editorial: The system landed the band exactly, at the bottom of the scale — the hardest place to be both accurate and humane. It found the two sections that genuinely work (the multi-Justice Erie canvass and the full Rule 23 walk) and named them before turning to the heavily weighted questions the student left blank or skipped. The skeptical judge added one correction the coaching draft had missed: the answer treated an interstate choice-of-law conflict as an Erie/Supremacy problem, and the published feedback says so.
bandRationale: Pairwise against the same-exam P reference: the P answer completes every question with real analysis — a full Celotex-based Q2 addressing both motions, a Q1 SMJ analysis that anchors Claim 1 and runs supplemental jurisdiction, and a Q4 with the Semtek MA/NH mutuality wrinkle. This student, by contrast, leaves Q2 (the second-most-weighted question) essentially blank, skips Q3, misses Q1's central 1367(b)/AIC core, and omits Q6's required original proposal. The student is clearly WEAKER than the P reference across the most heavily weighted questions. Against the same-exam H and DS references the gap is larger still — both canvass alternatives and resolve cores the student never reaches. Against the LP (different-year) reference the answer is COMPARABLE: the LP reference is complete but reaches wrong/conclusory results, while this student has genuinely competent patches (Erie in Q1, Q5) offset by outright skipped heavily-weighted cores (Q2, Q3) and an incomplete Q6. The LP signature — heavily weighted questions combining conclusory or skipped core analysis regardless of surface breadth — fits: Q2 skipped, Q1 SMJ core wrong, Q6 half-missing. The competent Erie and Q5 sections keep it at the top of the band.
whyNotHigher: Not P because the P reference and definition require issue recognition with cores that are underdeveloped rather than skipped; here the second-most-weighted question (Q2, 11 pts) is essentially blank, Q3 is skipped, Q6's required original proposal is missing, and Q1's controlling supplemental-jurisdiction/AIC issue and 12(b)(6) are absent. Too many heavily weighted cores are skipped or conclusory to merit P.
whyNotLower: This is already the weakest band.

feedback.headline: Genuine competence in the Erie and Rule 23 sections, but too many heavily weighted cores are skipped or conclusory
feedback.overview: Your answer shows real command in two spots — the multi-Justice Erie/Shady Grove canvass in Q1 and the full Rule 23 walk in Q5 — but the overall performance is dragged down because the second-most-weighted question (Q2) is essentially blank, Q3 is skipped, Q1's controlling supplemental-jurisdiction/AIC issue is missed, and Q6 omits its required original proposal. The through-line to fix is triage against point weights: the heaviest questions received the least developed analysis. This feedback prioritizes the moves that will most raise your next attempt.

strengths.detail: On the MRCP 4(a)(1)(H) attachment you actually ran the framework — outcome-determination, the Harlan primary-conduct test, and the Scalia/Ginsburg/Stevens Shady Grove positions — rather than just naming Erie. This is the most competent stretch of the answer and reads like real doctrinal engagement. (Note the caveat under improvements about not extending Erie to the substantive BD conflict.)

improvements.label: Q2 (11 pts) is essentially unanswered
improvements.whatHappened: You recited only the abstract summary-judgment standard and stopped. There is no resolution of the horizontal choice-of-law predicate that determines whether the MA-only Public Access defense even exists, no burden allocation, no application of the discovery record, and no separate treatment of the two motions.
improvements.whyItMatters: This is the second-most-weighted question. Leaving it blank forfeits a large share of available points regardless of how strong other sections are, and it is the single biggest driver of the band placement.
improvements.howToImprove: Even under time pressure, sequence it: first resolve which state's law governs the PAD (transferee court applies the transferor's choice-of-law rules; whether NH's first-restatement lex loci or MA's interest analysis, the harm points to MA), then allocate the trial burden to each movant, then apply the concrete record (FluNetwork report, Evans's testimony, video similarity) to show whether a genuine dispute exists on each of the two motions.

improvements.label: Q1 misses the controlling AIC/1367(b) supplemental-jurisdiction core
improvements.whatHappened: You aggregated the claims to reach the amount in controversy ('valued on entire amount claimed so million$ meets AIC') and never spotted that the count against Droobles is below $75K, nor ran the supplemental-jurisdiction inquiry under 1367(b)/Exxon. You also omitted the 12(b)(6) Twombly-Iqbal plausibility ground entirely.
improvements.whyItMatters: The AIC deficiency plus 1367(b) analysis is the central SMJ issue on a 25-point question, and the course materials treat the multiple-defendant/Rule 20 ouster as exactly the trap here. Aggregating claims against separate defendants is a rule error, not just an omission.
improvements.howToImprove: Separate each claim: identify the anchoring claim that independently satisfies 1332, then ask whether 1367(a) reaches the deficient claim and whether 1367(b) ousts it because the defendant was joined under Rule 20. Add a short 12(b)(6) paragraph applying plausibility to the allegations of Droobles' participation.

improvements.label: Q4 skips the Harry-vs-Ginny privity line and the Semtek transfer wrinkle
improvements.whatHappened: You invoked the right vocabulary (Parklane, Blonder-Tongue, Gonzalez) but opened with a category error ('CP doesn't apply to DD because can only be offensive posture'), never drew the outcome-controlling distinction between Harry (controlling shareholder, in privity) and Ginny (small stake, no privity), and omitted the Semtek MA-vs-NH mutuality question that decides Ginny's issue preclusion.
improvements.whyItMatters: Privity and which state's preclusion law governs after transfer are the two hinges of this question; without them the conclusions are asserted rather than reasoned, and the course expressly warns not to confuse claim and issue preclusion.
improvements.howToImprove: Run each defendant/plaintiff pairing line by line: for claim preclusion against Harry, analyze same-claim, final judgment, and privity via his control of HG; explain why Ginny is not in privity; then for Ginny's offensive nonmutual issue preclusion, use Semtek to pick MA (no mutuality) vs. NH (strict mutuality) and note it is outcome-determinative.

improvements.label: Q6 omits the required original proposal and the due-process hook
improvements.whatHappened: You developed the claim-preclusion expansion with pros and an extended access-to-justice critique, but never supplied the instruction's required second, original expansion, and the disadvantages drifted into criminal false-conviction and over-policing hypotheticals rather than the civil doctrine.
improvements.whyItMatters: The original proposal is an express requirement worth part of a 15-point question, and the model answers ground the critique in Mullane notice/due process and the FRCP 13/20/42 framework — the doctrinal anchors your essay is missing.
improvements.howToImprove: Add a distinct second expansion (e.g., broadening privity to bind represented nonparties) and analyze it separately. Tie disadvantages to notice/due process under Mullane and to consolidation limits under Rules 13/20/42 so the policy connects to course doctrine rather than general social commentary.

improvements.label: Q3 (appealability) effectively skipped
improvements.whatHappened: The only fragment ('If couldn't appeal, then likely not necessary to decision') appears misplaced from the preclusion discussion and does not address finality at all.
improvements.whyItMatters: Q3 is small (3 pts) but fully answerable with a compact checklist; leaving it blank forfeits easy points.
improvements.howToImprove: State the not-appealable path briefly: no final judgment under 1291 because damages are reserved, no Rule 54(b) certification, no 1292(b) or 1292(a)(1), no Cohen collateral order because liability goes to the merits, and no mandamus.

improvements.label: Q1 misframes the BD/Public-Access conflict as an Erie/Supremacy issue
improvements.whatHappened: After your (correct) Erie analysis of the summons rule, you wrote that the conflict between federal and MA business-disparagement law should also 'Use Eerie' and that the 'Supremacy clause for federal BD law vs MA BD law so fed law overrules state law.'
improvements.whyItMatters: The BD/PAD conflict is a horizontal (interstate) choice-of-law problem, not a vertical Erie/Supremacy problem — there is no federal statute competing with a state rule here. Misclassifying it leads to the wrong governing-law analysis, which in turn controls whether the MA-only Public Access defense exists (the pivot of Q2).
improvements.howToImprove: Reserve the Erie/Shady Grove framework for the state-procedure-vs-FRCP summons question. For the BD/PAD conflict, run horizontal choice of law: apply the forum's choice-of-law rules (Klaxon, plus the transferee-court wrinkle), then the R1 lex-loci or R2 interest analysis pointing to MA where the harm occurred.

revisionPlan: Budget words by point value before writing: Q1 (25), Q6 (15), and Q2 (11) should get the most ink; never let an 11-point question end at a bare rule statement.
For every SMJ question, separate each claim and each defendant and test AIC and 1367(a)/(b) individually before concluding diversity exists.
In summary-judgment and preclusion questions, resolve the choice-of-law predicate first (which state's substantive/preclusion law), then allocate burdens, then apply the record.
Keep vertical Erie analysis for state-procedure-vs-FRCP conflicts and horizontal choice of law (Klaxon, R1/R2) for competing state substantive laws; do not blend them.
In preclusion, go element by element and keep a distinct privity analysis for each party; identify which state's preclusion law governs under Semtek after any transfer.
In policy questions, complete every express instruction (here, the original proposal) and anchor pros/cons in named course doctrine (Mullane, Rules 13/20/42).
feedback.exampleRevision: On Q1 SMJ, instead of 'valued on entire amount claimed so million$ meets AIC,' analyze each claim separately: 'The HG v. Riddle claim (~$950K) independently satisfies 1332 and anchors the case. The claim against Droobles seeks only $50K, below the $75K threshold, so it needs supplemental jurisdiction. Under 1367(a) it forms part of the same case or controversy (the common deepfake scheme). But because Droobles is a second defendant who had to be joined under Rule 20, 1367(b) ousts supplemental jurisdiction over a plaintiff's Rule 20 claim in a diversity case — so, absent independent jurisdiction, that count must be dismissed even though the anchoring claim survives.' Note the contrast the course draws: a single defendant would not be joined via Rule 20, so the ouster would not apply.
feedback.closing: You clearly can do rigorous doctrinal work — the Erie canvass proves it. The fastest path to a higher band is not deeper analysis where you are already strong, but making sure every heavily weighted question gets a real, sequenced answer, and keeping the Erie and choice-of-law frameworks in their proper lanes. Practice triage against point values and complete the cores you are currently skipping.

judgeFindings.problem: In Q1 the student wrote 'Also conflict with federal business disparagement (BD) law and MA BD law... Use Eerie' and 'Supremacy clause for federal BD law vs MA BD law so fed law overrules state law.' This is a legal-rule error: the BD/PAD conflict is a horizontal (interstate) choice-of-law problem, not a vertical Erie/Supremacy problem. The draft's Erie praise is correctly targeted at the MRCP 4(a)(1)(H) attachment, but the draft does not flag the misapplication to the substantive tort conflict.
judgeFindings.correction: Add a low-priority note that the vertical Erie framework applies only to the state-vs-federal procedural summons rule; the federal-BD-vs-MA-BD conflict (and the MA-only Public Access defense) is resolved through horizontal choice of law (Klaxon plus R1/R2 analysis), not Supremacy.

editorial: This is the benchmark's worst band miss: the instructor graded the answer DS (the top band); the system placed it at a high P, two bands low. The disagreement is reasoned rather than random — the evaluator downgraded the answer for a conflated preclusion analysis and a skipped personal-jurisdiction path on heavily weighted questions, while the instructor evidently rewarded the answer's breadth and sophistication more heavily. This is exactly the kind of values judgment worth a lawyer's eye. Note also the second lesson here: the skeptical judge (step 6) caught the coaching draft telling the student their §1367(b) analysis was wrong when it was actually right, and corrected it before publication — the low QA score of 57 reflects that catch.
bandRationale: Pairwise against the same-exam references. Vs LP: the student is clearly stronger — LP's Q2 is essentially a blank statement of the SJ standard with no application, its Q3 is a misplaced non-answer, and its preclusion/class analyses are conclusory and disorganized, whereas the student develops all six questions with sound resolutions on Q1/Q2/Q3/Q5 and a substantial Q6. Student is well above LP. Vs P: roughly comparable — P edges the student on the IPJ effects test (Calder/Griffis) in Q1 and on running the happy-court transfer analysis in Q4, but both share the Harry/Ginny claim-preclusion conflation, and the student matches or slightly exceeds P on the thorough Erie framework and on the depth of the Q6 access-to-justice discussion. Vs H: the student is weaker — H distinguishes Harry from Ginny, runs the MA-vs-NH transfer question with Rios, and deploys the effects test explicitly, giving H a genuinely sounder preclusion core and richer IPJ. The student's Q4 defects and the IPJ application gap keep it from matching H's sustained soundness. The interval (comparable to P, below H) plus strong Q1/Q2/Q6 places it at the top of P.
whyNotHigher: Not H because the 8-point preclusion core is misframed (no Harry/Ginny privity split, no transfer/happy-court analysis, intersystem preclusion mislabeled as HCOL) and the heavily weighted Q1 IPJ path skips the intentional-tort/effects analysis — the H reference resolves both cores soundly, so the student does not reach comparable across-the-board soundness on the weighted questions.
whyNotLower: Not P-low or LP because every question is developed with mostly sound, correctly framed resolutions; Q1's Erie treatment, Q2's HCOL-then-Celotex sequencing, and Q6's access-to-justice canvassing are genuinely analytical rather than conclusory, decisively outperforming the LP reference and matching the P reference at its stronger end.

improvements.label: Distinguish Harry from Ginny for claim preclusion (Q4)
improvements.whatHappened: You treated the plaintiffs together, asserting that 'plaintiffs had control over the litigation in L1,' rather than analyzing privity separately for each. The central move is that Harry (65% controlling shareholder who controlled the HG litigation) is likely in privity, while a minority shareholder with no control is not.
improvements.whyItMatters: Privity is the pivot for whether claim preclusion runs at all, and it produces opposite results for the two plaintiffs. Collapsing them forfeits most of the analytical credit on the heaviest-weighted preclusion issue.
improvements.howToImprove: Split the analysis explicitly: for Harry, argue privity via controlling share and control over L1; for the minority plaintiff, argue no privity (small stake, no evidence of control), so claim preclusion cannot bind her and she remains free to litigate.

improvements.label: Do not label intersystem preclusion as 'HCOL' (Q4)
improvements.whatHappened: You wrote that you 'would do HCOL for mutuality using Semtek' and then simply selected NH law. The choice of which system's preclusion law applies is an intersystem-preclusion question, not a horizontal-choice-of-law question, and you skipped the transfer/'happy court' step that decides whether MA or NH preclusion law governs.
improvements.whyItMatters: The course materials expressly warn against conflating these ('this may sound like an Erie or HCOL issue, but it is not'). Whether MA (no mutuality) or NH (strict mutuality) law applies is outcome-determinative for whether the minority plaintiff can use non-mutual offensive issue preclusion.
improvements.howToImprove: Frame it as intersystem preclusion under Semtek/§1738, then run the transfer question: if venue and IPJ were proper, the transfer is a mere change of courthouse so MA preclusion law travels; MA's abolition of mutuality would let the non-party plaintiff use NMOCE, whereas NH's strict mutuality would bar it.
sources: Class 22 – Finish Issue Preclusion, Begin Intersystem Preclusion

improvements.label: Develop the intentional-tort/effects path for IPJ over Droobles (Q1)
improvements.whatHappened: Your specific-jurisdiction analysis for Droobles rested entirely on stream-of-commerce/no-advertising and reached 'no IPJ' without engaging the possibility that the tortious conduct was aimed at, and its harm felt in, MA.
improvements.whyItMatters: IPJ sits within the most heavily weighted question, and the effects/targeting angle is the strongest argument for jurisdiction over an out-of-state defendant in an intentional business-disparagement case. Omitting it leaves the analysis one-sided on a high-value issue.
improvements.howToImprove: Add a targeting/effects contact analysis: even without heavy MA sales, argue that conduct aimed at a MA business and causing harm felt in MA can support specific jurisdiction (cf. the 'targeted the forum' reasoning in the model answers), then weigh it against the fairness factors before concluding.

improvements.label: Add the notice/due-process objection to the policy essay (Q6)

improvements.whyItMatters: Notice/opportunity-to-be-heard is the strongest structural objection to expanding preclusion, and the reference answers foreground it as a distinct, high-value point.
improvements.howToImprove: Add a short paragraph that broader preclusion risks binding absent or unnotified parties without due process (Mullane), and connect it to the resource asymmetry you already flag (large parties can monitor dockets; individuals cannot).

In Q4, relabel the mutuality question as intersystem preclusion and add the transfer/happy-court step to choose between MA (no mutuality) and NH (strict mutuality) law before concluding on NMOCE.

feedback.exampleRevision: For Q4 claim preclusion, separate the plaintiffs: 'As to Harry, privity likely exists—his controlling (65%) share and control of the HG litigation make him effectively the same party, so claim preclusion (same transaction, final on-the-merits dismissal) can bind him. As to the minority shareholder, there is no privity: a small non-controlling stake with no evidence she directed L1 is insufficient, so claim preclusion does not reach her.' Then, for her issue-preclusion attempt, reframe the law-selection step: 'This is an intersystem-preclusion question, not HCOL. Under Semtek, the transferee court applies the preclusion law that would govern; if IPJ and venue were proper, the transfer is a mere change of courthouse and MA preclusion law travels. Because MA has abolished mutuality, she could assert non-mutual offensive issue preclusion on issues actually litigated and necessary in the SJ ruling; if instead NH law governs, its strict mutuality bars her.' This illustrates the analytical moves without supplying the full model answer.
feedback.closing: You are operating at a high level with disciplined structure and genuinely analytical work on the weighted questions. Note that your §1367 conclusion was correct—an earlier draft of this feedback wrongly suggested otherwise. Focus your next attempt on the preclusion core (splitting privity by plaintiff and correctly framing intersystem preclusion) and on rounding out the IPJ targeting/effects theory. Those targeted fixes address the specific gaps holding the answer back.

judgeFindings.problem: This is doctrinally wrong on these facts and contradicts both the instructor model answer and the cited course sources. The contamination/'AIC-deficiency is allowed' rule applies to the multi-PLAINTIFF, single-DEFENDANT scenario (P2 riding along), where §1367(b) does not textually apply. Here we have a SINGLE plaintiff (HG) suing MULTIPLE defendants, and Droobles is a defendant joined under Rule 20. §1367(b) therefore DOES textually bar HG's AIC-deficient claim against a Rule 20 defendant. The model answer expressly grounds the ouster in §1367(b) ('so 1367(b) prohibits supplemental jurisdiction (Exxon dictum)'), and the class-actions study aid confirms it: supplemental jurisdiction 'Does NOT work for multiple defendants (Rule 20 almost always applies; under 1367(b) ouster...).' The student's own reasoning ('a claim by a plaintiff against a party joined by Rule 20(a)(2)') is CORRECT. Worse, following the draft's advice (AIC deficiency 'does not trigger contamination, claim allowed') would flip the student to the wrong conclusion that the Droobles claim survives.
judgeFindings.correction: Remove improvement 4. The student's §1367(b) analysis is correct and should be credited, not criticized. Contamination theory is inapposite here because the deficient claim runs against a Rule 20 defendant, squarely within §1367(b)'s textual bar.
